Fonts and libraries Drift is built with

Every number in Drift comes from a small, fixed set of published models running on your phone. Estimates always carry a margin of error. The values below are the starting parameters; Drift personalizes them from your own nights.

Your need is tracked with a one-dimensional Kalman filter. It starts from the average for your age band and moves toward what you actually sleep on free nights, when no alarm cuts sleep short. Alarm nights only tell the filter that you needed at least that much.

The prior is the population mean for your age band (about 8 to 8.5 hours for young adults, lower for older adults) with a spread of about 0.6 hours. Free nights are corrected for rebound after debt (a factor of about 0.3). The estimate may drift by about 10 minutes of real change per month. Below five informative nights Drift shows the prior and says so.

string-array.name: st_meth_need_cites
string-array.item: Kalman, R. E. (1960). A new approach to linear filtering and prediction problems. Journal of Basic Engineering, 82(1), 35-45.
Hirshkowitz, M. et al. (2015). National Sleep Foundation\'s sleep time duration recommendations. Sleep Health, 1(1), 40-43.
Kitamura, S. et al. (2016). Estimating individual optimal sleep duration and potential sleep debt. Scientific Reports, 6, 35812.

resources.string: Debt is a leaky account over your last 14 sleep days. A night shorter than your need adds the shortfall. A longer night repays only part of the surplus. Older debt fades, so one bad week does not follow you forever.

The leak gives a half-life of about 7 days. Repayment starts at 60 percent of the surplus and is fitted to how quickly your own free-night rebound shrinks. Naps count fully up to 90 minutes and at half rate beyond that. Missing nights are filled from your same-weekday median and widen the margin. After three or more missing nights in a row Drift shows no debt rather than guessing.

string-array.name: st_meth_debt_cites
string-array.item: Van Dongen, H. P. A. et al. (2003). The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness. Sleep, 26(2), 117-126.
Banks, S. and Dinges, D. F. (2007). Behavioral and physiological consequences of sleep restriction. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 3(5), 519-528.

resources.string: The Sleep Regularity Index is the chance that you are in the same state, asleep or awake, at two moments exactly 24 hours apart. 100 means a perfectly repeating schedule. Drift also reports how widely your bedtime, wake time and mid-sleep vary.
Computed over 7 and over 14 days and only when at least five paired days exist. Timing spread uses circular standard deviation, so times around midnight are handled correctly.

string-array.name: st_meth_sri_cites
string-array.item: Phillips, A. J. K. et al. (2017). Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Scientific Reports, 7, 3216.

resources.string: Your chronotype is the middle of your sleep on free days, corrected for the extra sleep you take to repay debt (MSFsc). Social jetlag is how far your free-day midpoint sits from your work-day midpoint.
Until Drift has seen at least four free nights it blends your questionnaire answer with the data, weighting the data more with every night.

string-array.name: st_meth_chrono_cites
string-array.item: Roenneberg, T., Wirz-Justice, A. and Merrow, M. (2003). Life between clocks: daily temporal patterns of human chronotypes. Journal of Biological Rhythms, 18(1), 80-90.
Roenneberg, T. et al. (2007). Epidemiology of the human circadian clock. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 11(6), 429-438.
Wittmann, M. et al. (2006). Social jetlag: misalignment of biological and social time. Chronobiology International, 23(1-2), 497-509.

resources.string: Drift estimates when your melatonin starts to rise (dim light melatonin onset, DLMO) from when you habitually fall asleep. DLMO usually comes about 2 to 3 hours before habitual sleep onset. The melatonin window and the wind-down reminder are placed relative to it.

A circular Kalman filter follows your DLMO clock time from each night, giving less weight to alarm-driven and shift nights. After travel the estimate moves by at most about 1 hour per day eastward and 1.5 hours per day westward. The melatonin window is the hour starting about 2 hours after DLMO, and wind-down starts 1 hour before it.

string-array.name: st_meth_clock_cites
string-array.item: Pandi-Perumal, S. R. et al. (2007). Dim light melatonin onset (DLMO): a tool for the analysis of circadian phase in human sleep and chronobiological disorders. Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry, 31(1), 1-11.

resources.string: Your energy curve adds three processes: how much sleep pressure has built up while awake (homeostatic), where you are in your body clock cycle (circadian), and the grogginess just after waking (sleep inertia). It is normalized from 0 to 100 and split into phases such as morning peak, afternoon dip and wind-down. If the curve is too flat to show a real dip, Drift says so.

Sleep pressure is simulated over your last 14 days of sleep, falling while awake with a time constant of about 18 hours and recovering during sleep with about 4 hours. The circadian part is a 24 hour cosine plus a 12 hour harmonic that creates the post-lunch dip, tied to your DLMO. Sleep inertia decays over the first 1 to 2 hours after waking and is larger after short sleep. With 10 or more energy check-ins, a bounded fit adjusts the amplitude and phase.

string-array.item: Akerstedt, T. and Folkard, S. (1995). Validation of the S and C components of the three-process model of alertness regulation. Sleep, 18(1), 1-6.
Akerstedt, T. and Folkard, S. (1997). The three-process model of alertness and its extension to performance, sleep latency, and sleep length. Chronobiology International, 14(2), 115-123.
Borbely, A. A. (1982). A two process model of sleep regulation. Human Neurobiology, 1, 195-204.
Daan, S., Beersma, D. G. M. and Borbely, A. A. (1984). Timing of human sleep: recovery process gated by a circadian pacemaker. American Journal of Physiology, 246(2), R161-R183.
Tassi, P. and Muzet, A. (2000). Sleep inertia. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 4(4), 341-353.

resources.string: With no nights, Drift draws your curve from your answers and population averages and marks it Estimated. A few nights give a debt estimate with a wide margin. Around a week brings your personal sleep need and regularity. Two weeks or more switches on the full model.
Every number carries a label: Measured (read directly), Derived (calculated by fixed rules), Estimated (a model with a margin of error) or User-entered.
